facts.summary: Washington's minimum wage is $17.13 per hour effective January 1, 2026, far above the federal $7.25.
facts.sourceAgency: Washington State Department of Labor & Industries
facts.notes: State rate is adjusted annually for inflation each September 30, effective the following January 1. Some cities (e.g. Seattle, SeaTac, Tukwila) set higher local rates not captured here.

facts.summary: Washington follows the federal weekly overtime model (1.5x after 40 hours/week) and does not require daily overtime, except on certain public works projects.
facts.sourceAgency: Washington State Department of Labor & Industries
facts.notes: No daily OT threshold; the state difference from federal is the higher exempt salary floor recorded separately.

facts.summary: To be overtime-exempt as an executive/administrative/professional employee in 2026, Washington requires a salary of at least 2.25x the state minimum wage ($1,541.70/week, about $80,168/year), well above the federal $684/week.
facts.sourceAgency: Washington State Department of Labor & Industries
facts.notes: For 2026 both small (1-50) and large (51+) employers use 2.25x minimum wage = $1,541.70/week. Verify the current-year multiplier and figure, as it steps up on the annual L&I schedule.

facts.summary: Washington's Law Against Discrimination protects several classes beyond the federal set, including marital status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran/military status, citizenship/immigration status, and HIV/Hepatitis C status.
facts.notes: Listed classes are those in addition to the federally protected categories (race, color, national origin, sex, religion, age 40+, disability).

facts.summary: The Washington Law Against Discrimination covers employers with 8 or more employees, a lower threshold than Title VII's 15.
facts.sourceAgency: Washington State Legislature (Revised Code of Washington)
facts.notes: Definition excludes nonprofit religious or sectarian organizations.

facts.value: mandatory absent undue hardship; interactive process required
facts.summary: Washington Human Rights Commission rules require an employer to reasonably accommodate an 'able worker with a disability' -- through measures like job restructuring, a modified schedule, equipment, or reassignment to a vacant position -- unless the employer shows undue hardship, and require the employer to engage in an interactive process with the employee once an accommodation is requested.
facts.sourceAgency: Washington State Human Rights Commission (WAC Title 162)
facts.notes: Confirmed directly against the primary regulatory text (fetched from app.leg.wa.gov): 162-22-065 defines reasonable accommodation (enabling the application process, job performance, and equal benefits/privileges of employment); 162-22-075 sets the undue-hardship standard (cost/difficulty unreasonable given the employer's size and resources, ability to fold the cost into existing plans, and other legal/contractual constraints). Unlike NY/NJ/IL, this duty is set out in WSHRC administrative rules interpreting RCW 49.60.180 rather than spelled out in the RCW itself. Coverage follows WLAD's 8-employee threshold (see discrimination.coverage, above).

facts.summary: Whether an employee quits or is fired, Washington requires the employer to pay all wages owed by the end of the next regular pay period (no accelerated payment on discharge).
facts.sourceAgency: Washington State Legislature (Revised Code of Washington)
facts.notes: L&I enforces this rule; willful withholding of wages can expose an employer to a double-damages/exemplary-damages claim under RCW 49.52.070, not captured in this fact.

facts.summary: It is an unfair practice to discharge, expel, or otherwise discriminate against a person for opposing discrimination or for filing a charge, testifying, or assisting in a proceeding under the Law Against Discrimination.
facts.sourceAgency: Washington State Legislature (Revised Code of Washington)
facts.notes: Separate retaliation protections exist for wage complaints and other statutes; this fact captures the WLAD anti-retaliation provision.

facts.summary: L&I may not investigate or order payment for wage-payment violations that occurred more than three years before the wage complaint was filed.
facts.sourceAgency: Washington State Legislature (Revised Code of Washington)
facts.notes: Three-year lookback for L&I administrative wage complaints. Private civil actions for wages generally follow the RCW 4.16.080 three-year limitations period.

facts.summary: A discrimination complaint must be filed with the Washington State Human Rights Commission within 6 months of the alleged harm (12 months for pregnancy-related discrimination).
facts.notes: The full intake (submission, investigation, and signing of the perfected charge) must occur within the deadline. Longer periods apply to court actions.
